summary: Describes a framework for virtual private networks that run across IP backbones, covering the general concepts and requirements. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A virtual private network is a private network built over someone else's IP network, so a company keeps its own addressing and its own idea of who can reach whom. RFC 2764 sorts out what kinds of VPN there are, what each one needs, and which existing mechanisms could build it, so that different vendors' equipment can work together.

subtitle: What kinds of private network can be built over IP, and what each one needs to work

tldr.problem: Deploying private networks over IP backbones had been held up by the lack of interoperable implementations, which came from the lack of agreement on what a VPN is and from the number of different things all called a VPN.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a VPN as the emulation of a private wide area network using IP facilities, models it as a connectivity object rather like a physical network, and works through a taxonomy of four types: virtual leased line, virtual private routed network, virtual private dial network and virtual private LAN segment.
tldr.outcome: Each type is matched with the mechanisms that could implement it, and the memo ends with a short list of mechanisms worth standardising once so that the different types can share equipment and networks.

today: RFC 2764 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework rather than a specification, so the mechanisms it proposes had to be written up elsewhere, and its value today is as the map of the VPN types and their requirements.

sections.title: What a VPN Is and Why This Framework Exists
sections.content:
The memo describes a framework for virtual private networks running across IP backbones. It discusses the different types of VPN, their requirements, and proposes mechanisms that could implement each type using existing or proposed specifications. Its objective is to serve as a framework for related protocol development, so that the full set of specifications needed for interoperable VPN solutions can be written.

The motivation is stated plainly. There was significant interest in deploying VPNs over IP backbones, but widespread deployment had been hampered by the lack of interoperable implementations, which in turn came from the lack of general agreement on the definition and scope of a VPN and from confusion over the wide variety of solutions all described by the term. The memo's definition is deliberately narrow: a VPN is the emulation of a private wide area network facility using IP facilities, whether the public Internet or a private IP backbone. As there are as many types of WANs, there are as many types of VPNs, and that is the source of the confusion.

The way out is to model a VPN as a connectivity object. Hosts may attach to a VPN, and VPNs may interconnect with each other, in the same way hosts attach to physical networks and physical networks interconnect through bridges or routers. Addressing, forwarding, learning and advertising reachability, quality of service, security and firewalling all have common solutions across physical and virtual networks, so the introduction of VPNs does not create a need to reinvent networking. It is often useful to look at how a problem is solved in a physical network and apply the same principle where virtual and physical networks mix, extending the solution where necessary. Mechanisms that work across both make VPNs easier to introduce and reduce the work for standards and product development, because existing solutions can be reused.

The scope is IP backbones only, and the models are meant to apply to both IPv4 and IPv6. Native mappings onto switched backbones, such as LAN Emulation over ATM or Multiprotocol over ATM, are explicitly out of scope; where such protocols build the IP backbone, the VPNs discussed operate on top of that IP network. Native VPNs are restricted to the scope of the underlying backbone, whereas IP based VPNs can extend as far as IP reachability, and native VPN protocols are outside the scope of the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: A virtual private network is a private network built over someone else's IP network, so a company keeps its own addressing and its own idea of who can reach whom. RFC 2764 sorts out what kinds of VPN there are, what each one needs, and which existing mechanisms could build it, so that different vendors' equipment can work together.

sections.title: What Customers Expect of a VPN
sections.content:
Four requirements run through the whole framework. The first is opaque packet transport: the traffic carried inside a VPN may have no relation to the traffic on the IP backbone, either because it is multiprotocol or because the customer's own network uses addressing unrelated to the backbone's, in particular non-unique private addressing.

The second is data security, and here the memo describes two trust models. In one, the customer does not trust the provider to supply any security at all, and implements the VPN with customer premises equipment that includes firewall functionality, connected by secure tunnels, so the provider does nothing but carry IP packets. In the other, the customer trusts the provider to deliver a secure managed service, in the same way a customer trusts a public Frame Relay or ATM service, meaning the customer trusts that packets will not be misdirected, injected without authorisation, snooped on, modified in transit, or subjected to traffic analysis by unauthorised parties; providing firewalling and secure transport is then the provider's job. Different levels of security may be needed inside the provider backbone depending on the deployment: if the VPN traffic stays within a single provider's backbone, strong mechanisms such as IPsec may not be necessary for tunnels between backbone nodes, but if it crosses networks owned by several administrations they may be appropriate.

The third is quality of service. Leased and dial-up lines offer bandwidth and latency guarantees, and dedicated technologies such as ATM and Frame Relay have extensive mechanisms for similar guarantees, so as IP based VPNs spread there will be demand for the same, to keep applications working as they did. Whether an IP based VPN can offer them depends on the backbone underneath, but the framework still has to address how VPN systems use such capabilities as they evolve.

The fourth, the tunnelling mechanism, follows from the first two: VPNs must be implemented through some form of IP tunnelling, where the packet formats and addressing used inside the VPN can be unrelated to those used to route the tunnelled packets across the backbone. Such tunnels can provide some data security on their own, or that can be strengthened with other mechanisms such as IPsec.

Two further points frame the rest of the document. Most current implementations are based on customer premises equipment, ranging from firewalls to WAN edge routers and dedicated termination devices, bought and run by the customer or deployed and remotely managed by a provider. There is also interest in network based VPNs, where the operation of the VPN is outsourced to a provider and implemented on network rather than customer equipment; many mechanisms discussed apply to either, but some, such as piggybacking on routing protocols, are available only to providers. And an extranet, where two or more companies give each other limited access to their data, is really a policy decision: the control of who may access what, enforced at the interconnection points between domains by a firewall, a router with access lists, an application gateway or a similar device.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things are expected of any VPN. The traffic inside it may be anything, including private addresses that mean nothing outside the customer's network. It must be protected, and there are two ways to arrange that: the customer protects it end to end, or the provider promises to look after it. It should offer the same speed and delay guarantees a leased line did. And the first two of those together mean the traffic has to travel inside a tunnel, so that the backbone cannot see or confuse it.

sections.title: The Tunnel as the Building Block
sections.content:
An IP tunnel connecting two VPN endpoints is the basic building block from which many VPN services can be constructed. It operates as an overlay across the IP backbone, and the traffic sent through it is opaque to that backbone: in effect the backbone is being used as a link layer technology and the tunnel forms a point-to-point link. A VPN device may terminate several tunnels and forward packets between them and other interfaces, and the way it does so is what distinguishes the VPN types. The memo draws the analogy with three kinds of physical device: a two-port repeater forwards packets between its ports without examining them, a bridge forwards using MAC layer information in the packet, and a router forwards using layer 3 addressing. Each has a direct VPN analogue, and an IP tunnel is just another kind of link, which can be concatenated with another link or bound to a bridge or an IP forwarding table.

Several tunnelling mechanisms exist: IP-in-IP, GRE, L2TP, IPsec and MPLS. Each can carry frames opaquely across an IP network with forwarding kept separate from the address fields of the encapsulated packets, though MPLS is different in kind, since MPLS mechanisms apply only within an MPLS network, while IP based mechanisms extend as far as IP reachability. A VPN built directly on MPLS tunnelling therefore cannot extend beyond the MPLS network, in the same way an ATM mechanism such as LANE cannot extend outside ATM.

The requirements for a tunnelling protocol are then listed one by one. Multiplexing is needed when several tunnels must run between the same two IP endpoints, which happens in network based VPNs where one edge device serves many customers; a field is needed to tell which packets belong to which tunnel. L2TP has this through its tunnel-id and session-id fields, MPLS through its label, and IPsec through its Security Parameter Index. GRE has no multiplexing field of its own, though the key field meant for authenticating the source of a packet has sometimes been used as one, and IP-in-IP has none. Separately, the IETF and the ATM Forum have standardised a single format for a globally unique VPN identifier, which can be used in the control plane to bind a tunnel to a VPN at establishment, or in the data plane to identify the VPN of every packet so that packets for different VPNs can be aggregated over one tunnel.

Signalling is the other big requirement. Some configuration must be known in advance, such as the remote endpoint's IP address and the tunnel attributes such as the level of security wanted. The tunnel can then be established either by a management operation, for example through an SNMP Management Information Base that configures MPLS labels, source addresses for IP-in-IP or GRE tunnels, L2TP tunnel-ids and session-ids, or IPsec security association parameters, or by a signalling protocol that establishes tunnels dynamically. Signalling reduces the management burden and the management coordination needed when a VPN spans several administrative domains, and it lets mobile or intermittently connected nodes set up tunnels on demand. In a VPN environment it should be able to carry a VPN identifier, so that the tunnel can be tied to a particular VPN, and it should allow tunnel attributes such as frame sequencing or multiprotocol transport to be exchanged. Its role is only to negotiate those attributes, not to say how the tunnel will be used. L2TP, IPsec through IKE, and GRE as used with Mobile IP tunnelling all support a signalling protocol that could be adapted, and for MPLS there are two signalling protocols for establishing label switched paths: extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol called CR-LDP, and extensions to RSVP.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is built out of tunnels. A tunnel carries traffic the backbone cannot see, so the backbone can be treated as a link and the tunnel as the wire. The memo then lists what a tunnelling protocol has to do: tell apart several tunnels running between the same pair of machines, carry a VPN identifier so the right customer is picked out, set tunnels up dynamically rather than by hand, and negotiate whether the traffic inside is sequenced or carries several protocols. Existing protocols each cover part of this list.

sections.title: Four Kinds of VPN
sections.content:
The simplest is the virtual leased line. A point-to-point link is provided to the customer, connecting two customer premises devices. The link layer type used to connect those devices to the provider's nodes can be anything, an ATM virtual channel or a Frame Relay circuit, and the devices can be routers, bridges or hosts. Both provider nodes are connected to an IP network and an IP tunnel is set up between them; each node binds the stub link and the tunnel together at layer 2 and relays frames between them, taking the AAL5 payload and encapsulating it in an IPsec tunnel and vice versa. The contents are opaque to the node, which does not examine them, so to the customer it looks exactly like a single circuit, and the customer need not know that part of it runs over an IP backbone. If the two stub links are of different media types the node can no longer treat the traffic as opaque and must instead interwork between them, converting LLC/SNAP to NLPID, mapping between ARP variants and handling the media specific exchanges the customer devices expect.

A virtual private routed network is the emulation of a multi-site wide area routed network. Its distinguishing characteristic is that forwarding happens at the network layer. It consists of a mesh of IP tunnels between provider routers, with customer routers attached by stub links, and each provider router has a VPRN forwarding table holding network layer reachability information. The benefit is that the customer router sees the provider edge router as an ordinary neighbour and sends it everything with a default route; the tunnel mesh runs between the provider routers, not the customer routers, so tunnel establishment, maintenance and routing configuration are outsourced to the provider, and firewalling and quality of service processing are done by a few edge routers rather than many customer devices. New services can then be added without upgrading customer equipment, which matters for large numbers of residential subscribers, and the model resembles telephony, where a new service such as call waiting needs no change to the subscriber's equipment.

A virtual private dial network lets a remote user connect on demand through an ad hoc tunnel into another site. The user is on the public IP network over a dial-up or ISDN link and their packets are tunnelled across it, giving the impression of being directly connected to the site. Authentication is a prime requirement here, since anyone could try to reach such a site over a switched network. Because PPP connections and AAA systems are everywhere, any such system must in practice allow the near transparent reuse of them. L2TP is the protocol the memo focuses on: it extends user PPP sessions from an access concentrator to a remote network server, and it comes from two earlier protocols, L2F and PPTP, which is why it suits two different scenarios, compulsory tunnelling and voluntary tunnelling. L2TP multiplexes several calls over one link, with several tunnels between the same two endpoints identified by a tunnel-id and several sessions within a tunnel identified by a session-id; it has an inbuilt control connection for dynamic establishment; it carries the PPP security mechanisms along with the session; it does not protect its own control protocol, which needs IPsec or a similar mechanism; it transports PPP packets and so is multiprotocol because PPP is; it supports sequenced delivery, negotiable at session establishment and switchable by the network server during the session, and the sequence number also indicates dropped packets, which some PPP compression algorithms need; it has a keepalive to tell an outage from a long idle period; and it has no built-in segmentation and reassembly, so UDP/IP fragmentation applies, though the endpoints may lower the negotiated maximum receive unit to avoid it.

A virtual private LAN segment is the emulation of a LAN segment, sometimes called a transparent LAN service. It connects several stub customer nodes, bridges or routers, in a protocol transparent way, in the same way that LANE emulates a LAN over ATM. The benefits are complete protocol transparency, which matters for multiprotocol transport and for regulatory reasons in some provider contexts. Topologically it is like a VPRN except that each edge node bridges at the link layer rather than forwarding at the network layer, so most VPRN tunnelling and configuration mechanisms apply with the changes needed for link layer packets and addresses. It needs a broadcast capability, both for broadcast frames and for flooding a unicast frame whose destination address is unknown, and the address resolution protocols that run over a bridged network, such as ARP, rely on broadcast frames. Typical VPLSs will be fully meshed so that traffic between two nodes does not have to pass through a third, which would then need the spanning tree protocol for loop prevention.
sections.plainLanguage: Four shapes of VPN come out of the framework. A virtual leased line is a wire between two sites. A virtual private routed network is a mesh of sites that route packets between each other. A virtual private dial network is one user tunnelled into a site. A virtual private LAN segment is a fake LAN cable, so that the sites see each other's broadcast traffic. Each one needs a different kind of forwarding and a different place to put the tunnels.

sections.title: Summary of Recommendations
sections.content:
The memo points out that different VPN types share many requirements and mechanisms, and many networks will hold a mix of them, so it is useful to have as much commonality as possible; standardising a relatively small number of mechanisms lets a wide variety of VPNs be implemented. It then lists what should be examined carefully.

For IKE and IPsec: the transport of a VPN identifier when establishing a security association, a null encryption and null authentication option, multiprotocol operation, frame sequencing, asymmetric or legacy user authentication, and host address assignment and configuration. For L2TP: defining the modes of operation of IPsec when it is used to support L2TP. For VPNs generally: a VPN membership information configuration and dissemination mechanism that uses some form of directory or MIB, and making sure that solutions are applicable to different types of VPN rather than specific to one.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the four kinds of VPN will share equipment and often share a network, the memo argues for standardising the same few mechanisms everywhere. The short list is about telling tunnels which VPN they belong to, letting IPsec carry several kinds of traffic, and having one way to publish which sites belong to which VPN.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says security considerations are an integral part of any VPN mechanism, and that they are discussed in the sections describing those mechanisms, which is where the trust models, the tunnel security requirements and the per-type notes about data security appear. The security considerations section itself contains nothing further.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not have a separate list of security warnings, because it treats security as part of every mechanism it describes. The details are in the sections on tunnelling and on each kind of VPN.

items.title: Repeater
items.text: Forwards packets between its ports without examining them. The VPN counterpart is a tunnel bound as a point-to-point link.

items.title: Bridge
items.text: Forwards packets using the MAC layer information in the packet. The VPN counterpart is a virtual private LAN segment.

items.title: Router
items.text: Forwards packets using layer 3 addressing. The VPN counterpart is a virtual private routed network.
